title: Time domain non-linear quantum interferometry
authors: C. Fruy, A. Théry, B. Hue, W. Legrand, L. Jarjat, J. Craquelin, M. R. Delbecq, A. Cottet, T. Kontos
abstract: Interferometry is a powerful method for studying many fundamental phenomena ranging from gravitational waves to anyon excitations. Besides loss of coherence in the interferometer paths, quantum mechanics sets an incompressible bound for linear interferometry arising from the quantum noise of the light beam, called the shot noise limit. Here, we implement a non-linear quantum interferometer that uses a microwave cavity and a magnetic field resilient anharmonic superconducting quantum circuit made of granular aluminum. The circuit enables interferometry beyond the shot noise limit. A direct application of our findings is the detection of dark matter (axions or dark photons), high-frequency gravitational waves or astronomical masers.
summary: This paper demonstrates a non-linear quantum interferometer built using a superconducting circuit coupled to a microwave cavity. By exploiting anharmonicity, the system surpasses the shot noise limit, enabling the detection of extremely weak signals. The authors compare two measurement protocols, achieving high sensitivity for applications like dark matter detection.
main_problem: The primary goal is to implement and characterize a non-linear quantum interferometer capable of surpassing the standard quantum limit (shot noise limit) for detecting extremely weak quantum signals.
main_result: The non-linear superconducting circuit enables the detection of weak signals down to photon numbers as low as $10^{-5}$, demonstrating a high figure of merit comparable to single-photon detectors.
method: The study employs two distinct interferometric protocols (Protocol A and Protocol B) using Ramsey sequences on a superconducting circuit coupled to a microwave cavity.
model_or_system: The physical platform is a microwave cavity quantum electrodynamics (cQED) system utilizing a granular aluminum (grAl) Josephson junction circuit, which provides the necessary anharmonicity for non-linear effects.
key_observables: The key observables include the shift in Ramsey interference fringes, the diameter of the signal in the I-Q plane ($d_{IQ}$), and the measured frequency shift ($\Delta f_q$).
important_parameters: Key parameters include the weak signal photon number ($n_w$), the measurement time ($t$), and the achievable sensitivity limit ($n_{w,lim} \approx 10^{-5}$).
main_assumptions: Assumptions include the validity of the input-output formalism, the characterization of the cross-Kerr parameter ($K_a q$), and acknowledging measurement-induced dephasing effects.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the principle of the non-linear interferometer, the evolution of Ramsey fringes as a function of the weak signal phase ($\phi_w$), and quantitative comparisons between Protocol A and Protocol B performance versus integration time.
paper_structure: The paper details the theoretical framework (Hamiltonian, input-output formalism), presents two measurement protocols (A and B) for signal extraction, calibrates the measurement apparatus, and compares the sensitivity and scaling laws of both protocols.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it pushes the boundaries of quantum measurement techniques in superconducting circuits, directly addressing noise limitations in quantum sensing using non-linear quantum optics.
